comments.author: deng
comments.text:
Nowadays, I just get old laptops with broken screens and take the mainboard out. They are dirt cheap, often even have 16GB of RAM, you can just dump pretty much any linux on them and they are usually way faster than Pis.
The boards are of course bigger, which I guess will be a non-starter for many. They'll also require active cooling unless you downclock them considerably. They often also require more power, although many mainboards can be configured down two a few watts of power consumption, depending on what peripherals and speed you need.
Yeah, it's more work than just getting a Pi, but given the current prices, it makes sense for me.

comments.author: asciimike
comments.text:
The viability of space DCs seem to depend entirely on the existence of higher latency, lower throughput, single card to single server workloads, which IMO isn't the primary class of workload today (and if one holds the belief that frontier will maintain their dominant position, this will remain rack/row/facility level, which isn't viable for orbital facilities to handle).
If that workload does expand in usage, and the economics of orbital DCs make sense (with high launch costs, zero ability to do maintenance, and weight penalties for shielding and radiators), then surely ocean based data centers (e.g. Panthalassa) make more sense (lower 'launch' costs, high latency on maintenance, no weight penalties), and if those make sense then surely the distributed land based facilities (e.g. Rune Energy) or home based facilities (e.g. Span XFRA) make even more sense (easier maintenance, low/no permitting overhead because they're covered by existing permits, reasonable quality terrestrial fiber internet).

comments.author: pu_pe
comments.text:
The article makes several big assumptions that are questionable (experimental cooling can scale, permit issues on land will only become worse, etc). But more importantly, their analysis of the risks of placing a data center in orbit is completely off. They mention that it costs tens of millions to launch a missile to destroy a satellite, and it might be cheaper to simply replace it (based on launch costs). We can also assume that placing big fat valuable targets in space would have many actors wondering how to make it cheaper to destroy them.
For those reasons alone, and because compute will become more and more strategic for defense, I find it very hard to believe that data centers in space will represent even 5% of all compute in the next 10 years. I think a higher proportion will rather be underground or in bunkers than in space.

comments.author: a4isms
comments.text:
My very first professional gig in the mid-80s was on a classified ad-taking application for what were then called penny-savers, physical newspaper-like publications that were nearly 100% classifieds. Penny-savers would be distributed in boxes around urban centres and could be very profitable. Our app ran on MP/M, a multi-user CP/M variant. And when it was time to go to print, our code generated PS directly, there was no "printer driver" or abstraction of any kind.
We sold our customers
two
Apple LaserWriters each, because if one went down just before going to print they'd be screwed. We would print on both in parallel for speed, but could fall back to just one. And the printed ads? Somebody over in the print shop would cut them out in strips and then paste those strips up to be photographed for the printing press. We didn't have full end-to-end digital yet.
PS wasn't easy, but it was very grokkable.

comments.author: tonyedgecombe
comments.text:
My retirement project is a PostScript interpreter. I've done about 260 of the 286 operators in the original Apple LaserWriter. I'm about half way through the last tricky bit, Type 1 fonts.
The internals are quite interesting, I always assumed the interpreter just processed the input as it arrives but it actually starts a PostScript program as soon as the printer boots and that controls the hardware and handling incoming jobs. A lot of this code is available through a console, ie:
userdict begin /start load == end
dumps the first program started by the printer.
I have an original LaserWriter which works through the console but doesn't print. Luckily someone has done the work to get the firmware running in MAME.
My interest in this came from working with a QMS distributor in the eighties. At the time I didn't really have a chance to delve that deep into the technology but I was always fascinated by it.

is

Mainly I learned that Ghostscript is doing a lot to make its PostScript interpreter fast: with the non-graphical test programs I could think up, GhostScript was many times faster interpreting the program (even computationally intensive ones) than my runtime (called "egon") could execute the byte-compiled PostScript.  So it was a computation fail but still a pedagogy win.
I've always been meaning to learn more about how Ghostscript is engineered.

beforehand
